_doc: The 2026-11-14 adversarial review of the skills' "I can" statements: every finding (key, stage, severity, problem, the statement as it was, why, the reviewer's correction, its source with url, date and quotation) and its outcome. applied: the changes made (reworded, moved to another stage under a new key, or added as a new key) with the words now in data/i18n/en.json; rejected: the reason. The README in this folder is the readable form. crates/humanity-systems/src/skills/statement_review_tests.rs holds the data to it.

findings.statement: I can check whether a person is responding and breathing, and place them in the recovery position.
findings.why: Read literally, the check always ends in the recovery position, whatever it finds. A person who is unresponsive and NOT breathing normally (occasional gasps are common early in cardiac arrest and do not count) needs an emergency call and CPR at once; rolling them into the recovery position instead delays CPR. The recovery position is only for someone unresponsive but breathing normally. St John Ambulance's CPR page (clinically reviewed 2026-09-18, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/cpr/): "Ignore occasional, irregular gasps - these are common in the early stages of cardiac arrest." and "If they are not breathing normally, start CPR".
findings.correct: I can check whether a person is responding and breathing normally. If they are unresponsive but breathing normally, I put them in the recovery position and keep checking their breathing; if they are not breathing normally (gasps do not count), I call the emergency number and start CPR.

source.quote: It’s safe to place someone in the recovery position who is not responding to you but is breathing normally.

changes.text: I can check whether a person is responding and breathing normally. If they are unresponsive but breathing normally, I put them in the recovery position and keep checking their breathing; if they are not breathing normally (gasps do not count), I call the emergency number and start CPR.

findings.statement: I can do chest compressions and rescue breaths on a practice dummy at the right pace.
findings.why: "At the right pace" gives the learner nothing to check, and depth, the compression-to-breath ratio and the defibrillator are missing. No stage of the first aid ladder mentions a defibrillator (AED) at all, though sending for one is part of every basic life support sequence. Same page: "press down hard, to a depth of about five-six centimetres", "after 30 compressions, provide two rescue breaths" and "ask a helper to find and bring a defibrillator, if available."
findings.correct: I can give chest compressions on a practice manikin about 5 to 6 cm deep at 100 to 120 a minute, with 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, send someone for a defibrillator, and follow a training defibrillator's spoken instructions.

source.quote: Push at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute.

changes.text: I can give chest compressions on a practice manikin about 5 to 6 cm deep at 100 to 120 a minute, with 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, send someone for a defibrillator, and follow a training defibrillator's spoken instructions.

findings.statement: I can cool a burn with clean running water and cover it loosely.
findings.why: The statement leaves out how long to cool, the one number that decides whether cooling works; people commonly cool for a few seconds. It also does not warn off ice, creams or butter, or say to take off rings before swelling starts. Same page: "Do not use ice, creams or gels. They may cause damage and increase the risk of infection." and "Remove any jewellery or clothing, unless stuck to the burn, before the area begins to swell." and "When the burn has cooled, cover the area loosely with cling film, lengthways."
findings.correct: I can cool a burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes (never ice, creams or butter), take off rings or clothing near it before it swells unless they are stuck, and then cover it loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.

source.quote: Hold it under cool running water for at least 20 minutes or until the pain feels better.

changes.text: I can cool a burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes (never ice, creams or butter), take off rings or clothing near it before it swells unless they are stuck, and then cover it loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.

findings.statement: I can press firmly on a bleeding wound with a clean cloth and keep the pressure on.
findings.why: Missing two basic precautions: protecting yourself from blood (gloves if you have them) and getting someone to call the emergency number for severe bleeding. Same page: "Ask a helper to call 999 or 112 for emergency help."
findings.correct: I can put on gloves if I have them, get someone to call the emergency number for heavy bleeding, and press firmly on the wound with a clean pad, keeping the pressure on.

source.quote: With open wounds there's a risk of infection, so wear protective first aid gloves (if available)

changes.text: I can put on gloves if I have them, get someone to call the emergency number for heavy bleeding, and press firmly on the wound with a clean pad, keeping the pressure on.

findings.statement: I can spot shock, heat illness and cold injury and begin the right care while help comes.
findings.why: "Begin the right care" covers three different conditions and says nothing a learner can check. Heatstroke in particular is an emergency: call for help and cool the person straight away. Same page: "Sit them down and wrap them in a cool, wet sheet."
findings.correct: I can spot shock, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and cold injuries such as hypothermia and frostbite, and give the first steps for each while help comes; for heatstroke I call the emergency number and start cooling the person at once with a cool, wet sheet or cold water.

source.quote: Call 999 or 112 for emergency help.

changes.text: I can spot shock, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and cold injuries such as hypothermia and frostbite, and give the first steps for each while help comes; for heatstroke I call the emergency number and start cooling the person at once with a cool, wet sheet or cold water.

findings.statement: I can enter shallow water with a helper nearby, float on my back and breathe out into the water.
findings.why: A helper "nearby" is not enough for someone who cannot swim yet: people learning to swim slip under silently, and drowning prevention asks for close, constant watching by someone able to help. The same page also says: "Life jackets can also be used by weaker swimmers of all ages in and around natural water and swimming pools."
findings.correct: I can enter shallow water with a helper who can swim watching me closely the whole time and staying within reach, float on my back and breathe out into the water.

source.quote: Designate a responsible adult to supervise closely and constantly when children are in or near water (including bathtubs).

changes.text: I can enter shallow water with a helper who can swim watching me closely the whole time and staying within reach, float on my back and breathe out into the water.

findings.statement: I can help someone in trouble using a rope, pole or floating object while staying on dry ground.
findings.why: The words are right (reach or throw, stay on dry ground), but they sit at Proficient (level 8), so a learner from Novice to Competent is never taught the rule that keeps would-be rescuers alive, and the most common instinct, jumping in, is what drowns rescuers. It also leaves out calling for help first. The page's steps: "SHOUT", "REACH", "THROW", and "DON'T GO – Never enter the water yourself, no matter what."
findings.correct: move to beginner, reworded: I can call the emergency number and help someone in trouble in the water by shouting to them, reaching with a pole or rope, or throwing something that floats, without ever going into the water myself.

source.quote: Never enter the water to attempt a rescue; instead, use the advice below and call 999 as soon as possible.

changes.text: I can call the emergency number and help someone in trouble in the water by shouting to them, reaching with a pole or rope, or throwing something that floats, without ever going into the water myself.

findings.statement: I can climb a fixed ladder with three points of contact while a helper steadies the base.
findings.why: A fixed ladder is part of the building or structure, so "a helper steadies the base" does not apply to it; the helper steadying the base belongs to a portable ladder, whose real Novice lesson is setting it on firm, level ground and facing it while climbing. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1050 (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.1050): a fixed ladder "means a ladder that cannot be readily moved or carried because it is an integral part of a building or structure." The QuickCard also says: "Use a ladder only on a stable and level surface".
findings.correct: I can climb a short portable ladder set on firm, level ground, facing it and keeping three points of contact, while a helper steadies the base.

source.date: OSHA 3246 Portable Ladder Safety QuickCard (file dated 2020-09-28)
source.quote: Always maintain a 3-point (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand) contact on the ladder when climbing.

changes.text: I can climb a short portable ladder set on firm, level ground, facing it and keeping three points of contact, while a helper steadies the base.

source.date: OSHA 3246 Portable Ladder Safety QuickCard (file dated 2020-09-28)

findings.statement: I can climb a route at my level on a rope with a belayer, calling clearly to my partner.
findings.why: The ladder puts the learner on a rope with a belayer at Proficient and leading at Expert, but no stage ever teaches belaying, the skill that holds a partner's life and the first thing a roped climber is asked to do in return. A missing prerequisite: belaying is learned on a course, with the brake hand never leaving the rope. The DAV booklet also says: "Partner check before every climb".
findings.correct: add at competent: I can belay a partner on a top rope after learning on a course, with one hand always on the brake side of the rope, and do a partner check before every climb.

source.quote: One hand always holding on to the brake side of the rope.

changes.text: I can belay a partner on a top rope, having learned on a course, with one hand always on the brake side of the rope.

findings.note: The partner check in the reviewer's words is left out because Competent's s3_b already says it (check my partner's knot and harness, and be checked by them).

findings.statement: I can compare the possible causes of a set of symptoms and say what to watch for next.
findings.why: Comparing the possible causes of symptoms is diagnosis. A lay carer's own short list can falsely reassure and delay care for something serious (a stroke, sepsis, a heart attack), and in the US offering diagnoses to others is the practice of medicine, which state law reserves to licensed practitioners. The safe lay skill is to observe, describe and know the warning signs that mean get help now. (No US state statute could be read for the quotation: see the summary.)
findings.correct: I can describe a person's symptoms clearly and in order to a health worker, check a trusted health service's list of warning signs, and know which signs mean get help now, leaving the diagnosis to a qualified professional.

source.quote: the decision about return to sports is a medical decision that should be made by a healthcare provider.

changes.text: I can describe a person's symptoms clearly and in order to a health worker, check a trusted health service's list of warning signs, and know which signs mean get help now, leaving the diagnosis to a qualified professional.

findings.statement: I can trace where a water or waste system is failing and isolate or fix the problem.
findings.why: Tracing a failing waste system leads to septic tanks, pits and manholes, which are confined spaces whose gases can kill within minutes, and would-be rescuers die with the first victim. The statement gives no warning. NIOSH Alert 86-110 (January 1986, https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/209448): "It is noted that 60 percent of the deaths in confined spaces involve potential rescuers."
findings.correct: I can trace where a water or waste system is failing from the outside and isolate or fix simple faults, without ever climbing or leaning into a tank, pit or manhole (its gases can kill in minutes), and I call a qualified plumber or the water authority for anything more.

source.quote: Has limited or restricted means for entry or exit (for example, tanks, vessels, silos, storage bins, hoppers, vaults, and pits are spaces that may have limited means of entry.)

changes.text: I can trace where a water or waste system is failing from the outside and isolate or fix simple faults, without ever climbing or leaning into a tank, pit or manhole (its gases can kill in minutes), and I call a qualified plumber or the water authority for anything more.

findings.statement: I can wash my hands properly with soap and clean water at the moments that matter.
findings.why: "Properly" and "the moments that matter" cannot be checked. The CDC gives a time and a list (before, during and after preparing food, after the toilet, after touching animals or waste, before and after caring for someone who is sick).
findings.correct: I can wash my hands with soap and clean running water, scrubbing the backs, between the fingers and under the nails for at least 20 seconds, before handling food and after the toilet, touching animals or waste, or caring for someone who is sick.

source.quote: Scrub your hands for at least 20 seconds.

changes.text: I can wash my hands with soap and clean running water, scrubbing the backs, between the fingers and under the nails for at least 20 seconds, before handling food and after the toilet, touching animals or waste, or caring for someone who is sick.

findings.statement: I can clean, then disinfect, a surface touched by raw meat or a sick person.
findings.why: Disinfecting invites mixing products; bleach mixed with ammonia or other cleaners gives off a poisonous gas. The statement should carry that warning.
findings.correct: I can clean, then disinfect, a surface touched by raw meat or a sick person, using one disinfectant as its label says and never mixing bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.

source.quote: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.

changes.text: I can clean, then disinfect, a surface touched by raw meat or a sick person, using one disinfectant as its label says and never mixing bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.

findings.statement: I can set up hand washing and waste disposal for a camp or small group.
findings.why: The number that matters most in camp sanitation, how far waste goes from water, is missing, so a learner can "set up" a latrine beside a stream and still tick the box. The same page: "carry water 200 feet away from streams or lakes and use small amounts of biodegradable soap."
findings.correct: I can set up hand washing and waste disposal for a camp or small group, with latrines or catholes 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep and at least 200 feet (about 60 m) from water, camp and trails, and washing water carried the same distance from streams.

source.quote: deposit solid human waste in catholes dug 6 to 8 inches deep, at least 200 feet from water, camp and trails.

changes.text: I can set up hand washing and waste disposal for a camp or small group, with latrines or catholes 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep and at least 200 feet (about 60 m) from water, camp and trails, and washing water carried the same distance from streams.

findings.statement: I can clear a safe spot, keep water and a shovel near, and light a fire with a lighter or match under an adult's eye.
findings.why: Lighting a fire is banned or restricted in many places and seasons, but the ladder only asks the learner to "judge whether fire is allowed" at Competent (s3_b), after lighting fires since Novice. "Clear a safe spot" has no size a learner can check, and "under an adult's eye" assumes the learner is a child. The same page: "ensure you have at least a 10-foot diameter around the site" and "Stay at least 15 feet from tents, vegetation, and low-hanging branches."
findings.correct: I can check that fires are allowed here today, use an existing fire ring or clear a circle at least 10 feet (3 m) across and at least 15 feet (4.5 m) from tents, plants and low branches, keep water and a shovel near, and light a fire with a lighter or match while an experienced person watches.

source.quote: Don’t build a campfire or dig a fire pit if the campground, area, event rules, or local laws prohibit them.

changes.text: I can check that fires are allowed here today, use an existing fire ring or clear a circle at least 10 feet (3 m) across and at least 15 feet (4.5 m) from tents, plants and low branches, keep water and a shovel near, and light a fire with a lighter or match while an experienced person watches.

findings.statement: I can put a fire fully out until the ashes are cold to the touch.
findings.why: It gives the end state but not the method, and "cold to the touch" invites touching ashes that can still burn. The same page: "Pour lots of water on the fire until the hissing sound stops, drowning all the embers" and "If your campfire is too hot to touch, it’s too hot to leave."
findings.correct: I can put a fire fully out by drowning it with water until the hissing stops, stirring the ashes and drowning them again, then holding the back of my hand over them to check that no heat is left.

source.quote: Hover the back of your hand over the ashes to feel that the embers are cool

changes.text: I can put a fire fully out by drowning it with water until the hissing stops, stirring the ashes and drowning them again, then holding the back of my hand over them to check that no heat is left.

findings.statement: I can burn wood into charcoal for the kiln with a steady method.
findings.why: Making charcoal means burning wood with little air, which gives off carbon monoxide; it must be done outdoors and away from buildings, never in a shed, garage or tent. "A steady method" is also too vague to check.
findings.correct: I can burn wood into charcoal outdoors, well away from buildings and never in an enclosed space (it gives off carbon monoxide), using a pit, drum or kiln method I can describe step by step.

source.quote: Never burn charcoal indoors.

changes.text: I can burn wood into charcoal outdoors, well away from buildings and never in an enclosed space (it gives off carbon monoxide), using a pit, drum or kiln method I can describe step by step.

findings.statement: I can put out a small fire with a blanket or the correct extinguisher.
findings.why: "A small fire" cannot be checked, and the statement does not repeat the conditions for fighting a fire at all (others alerted, the fire service called, an escape route behind you, clear of the smoke). The USFA lists them, and adds: "alert others, leave the building, and call 911".
findings.correct: I can put out a fire with a fire blanket or the correct extinguisher (pull, aim low, squeeze, sweep), only when others have been alerted, the fire service has been called, the fire is small and contained to one object such as a pan or a bin, I am clear of the smoke and I have an escape route behind me.

source.quote: Is the fire small and contained in a single object or to a surface (like a pan or a wastebasket)?

changes.text: I can put out a fire with a fire blanket or the correct extinguisher (pull, aim low, squeeze, sweep), only when others have been alerted, the fire service has been called, the fire is small and contained to one object such as a pan or a bin, I am clear of the smoke and I have an escape route behind me.

findings.statement: I can decide when to shelter, and when to leave, during a solar storm.
findings.why: True for astronauts and spacecraft (the game's ship), but misleading as a real-life skill: a solar radiation storm is no radiation hazard to people on the ground. NOAA's scale (https://www.spaceweather.gov/noaa-scales-explanation, 2026-11-11) lists the biological effects of the worst storm, S5, only as "Unavoidable high radiation hazard to astronauts on EVA (extra-vehicular activity)" and risk to "passengers and crew in high-flying aircraft at high latitudes". A real-life learner could come away thinking they should shelter from solar storms. In a real radiation emergency the action is to get inside and stay inside: CDC (https://www.cdc.gov/radiation-emergencies/response/get-inside.html, 2024-04-15): "Staying inside for at least 24 hours can protect you and your family until it is safe to leave the area."
findings.correct: In the game: I can decide when to go to the ship's storm shelter, and when to leave it, during a solar storm. In real life: I can say that solar storms are a radiation hazard to astronauts and high-flying aircrew, not to people on the ground, and in a radiation emergency I get inside, stay inside for at least 24 hours and follow official instructions.

source.quote: far too small to produce an observable health effect.

changes.text: I can decide when to go to the ship's storm shelter, and when to leave it, during a solar storm.

I can explain that solar storms are a radiation danger to astronauts and high-flying aircrew, not to people on the ground, and in a radiation emergency I get inside, stay inside for at least 24 hours and follow official instructions.

findings.note: The reviewer's one statement with "In the game:" and "In real life:" halves is split into two statements, each starting "I can" like every other.

findings.statement: I can free a person from simple dangers, such as a fallen branch or a stuck door, without being hurt myself.
findings.why: After a storm, a fallen branch may be touching or energized by a downed power line, and circuits do not always switch off. Freeing someone from it without checking can kill both people. The same fact sheet: "Downed wires can energize other nearby objects, such as fences, water pipes, bushes and trees" and "Never go near a downed or fallen electric power line."
findings.correct: I can free a person from simple dangers, such as a fallen branch or a stuck door, after checking that no power line is down or touching it, and without being hurt myself; if a line is down, I keep everyone away and call the emergency number.

source.quote: Circuits do not always turn off when a power line falls into a tree or onto the ground.

changes.text: I can free a person from simple dangers, such as a fallen branch or a stuck door, after checking that no power line is down or touching it, and without being hurt myself; if a line is down, I keep everyone away and call the emergency number.

findings.statement: I can keep a safe distance from wildlife and never feed or touch wild animals.
findings.why: "A safe distance" cannot be checked, and the distance people guess is usually far too short. National parks give numbers; the same page adds: "and at least 25 yards (23 m) away from all other animals, including bison and elk."
findings.correct: I can stay at least 100 yards (91 m) from bears, wolves and big cats and at least 25 yards (23 m) from other large animals, or further where local rules say so, and never feed or touch wild animals.

source.quote: Always stay at least 100 yards (91 m) away from bears, wolves, and cougars

changes.text: I can stay at least 100 yards (91 m) from bears, wolves and big cats and at least 25 yards (23 m) from other large animals, or further where local rules say so, and never feed or touch wild animals.

findings.statement: I can find and describe footprints, droppings and feeding signs.
findings.why: Examining droppings invites handling them, and animal droppings carry parasites (raccoon roundworm eggs among them) that infect people who get them on their hands and then into their mouths. The same page: "People become infected by consuming infectious eggs."
findings.correct: I can find and describe footprints, droppings and feeding signs without touching droppings with bare hands, and I wash my hands afterwards.

source.quote: Most infections are in children and others who are more likely to put dirt or animal waste in their mouth by mistake.

changes.text: I can find and describe footprints, droppings and feeding signs without touching droppings with bare hands, and I wash my hands afterwards.

findings.statement: I can spar lightly with control, defending as often as I attack, and stop at once when my partner taps or calls it.
findings.why: Light sparring still brings blows to the head. The statement has no coach present and no rule for a knock to the head; concussion guidance is to stop at once and not return until a health professional says so. The same page: "the decision about return to sports is a medical decision that should be made by a healthcare provider."
findings.correct: I can spar lightly with control under a coach's eye, defending as often as I attack, stop at once when my partner taps or calls it, and stop for the day and get checked if either of us takes a hard knock to the head or feels dizzy or confused.

source.quote: Remove the athlete from sports participation right away if a concussion is suspected.

changes.text: I can spar lightly with control under a coach's eye, defending as often as I attack, stop at once when my partner taps or calls it, and stop for the day and get checked if either of us takes a hard knock to the head or feels dizzy or confused.

findings.statement: I can use a tool such as an axe or hammer for its real job, such as splitting wood, with control and a clear work area.
findings.why: Splitting wood is a common cause of foot, leg and eye injuries, and the statement names no protective gear or footing. The same manual: "Always wear good, stout leather boots, at least 8–inches high." and "Stand with your weight evenly distributed with both feet planted about shoulder width apart."
findings.correct: I can use an axe or hammer for its real job, such as splitting wood, wearing safety glasses and stout boots, with secure footing, feet about shoulder width apart, my spare hand clear of the blade and nobody near me.

source.date: USDA Forest Service MTDC 9923-2823P (1999; no date on the page)
source.quote: Always wear safety glasses or goggles for eye protection.

changes.text: I can use an axe or hammer for its real job, such as splitting wood, wearing safety glasses and stout boots, with secure footing, feet about shoulder width apart, my spare hand clear of the blade and nobody near me.

source.date: USDA Forest Service MTDC 9923-2823P (1999; no date on the page)

findings.statement: I can fit and look after my gear, such as the bowstring and arrows, and spot damage before it becomes dangerous.
findings.why: Gear care leaves out the best-known way a bow breaks and hurts its archer: dry-firing, releasing a drawn string with no arrow. It belongs with looking after the gear.
findings.correct: I can fit and look after my gear, such as the bowstring and arrows, spot damage before it becomes dangerous, and never dry-fire a bow (draw and release it without an arrow).

source.quote: Never dry-fire a bow – drawing and releasing the string without a nocked arrow.

changes.text: I can fit and look after my gear, such as the bowstring and arrows, spot damage before it becomes dangerous, and never dry-fire a bow (draw and release it without an arrow).

findings.statement: I can shoot from other positions, such as kneeling, and at moving or unmarked targets with a safe backstop.
findings.why: "Unmarked targets" is ambiguous: meant as targets at unknown distances, it can be read as shooting at something not yet identified, which breaks the rule to be sure of your target. The same page: "Don’t shoot over a ridge if you can’t see what’s on the other side."
findings.correct: I can shoot from other positions, such as kneeling, and at moving targets or targets at distances I have to judge myself, always sure of my target and of what is in front of and behind it, with a safe backstop.

source.quote: Take the time to make sure of your target before you shoot, and take note of what’s in front of and behind your target.

changes.text: I can shoot from other positions, such as kneeling, and at moving targets or targets at distances I have to judge myself, always sure of my target and of what is in front of and behind it, with a safe backstop.

findings.statement: I can treat every firearm as loaded, keep the muzzle in a safe direction, keep my finger off the trigger and know my backstop.
findings.why: Only three and a half of the four basic firearm safety rules: "know my backstop" covers what is beyond the target but not being certain of the target itself, and "keep my finger off the trigger" lacks "until I am ready to shoot". It also does not say that a novice handles firearms only with a qualified instructor. The same release lists: "Treat every firearm as if it is loaded.", "Always control the muzzle of your firearm." and "Never touch a trigger until you are ready to shoot at a game animal or a safe target."
findings.correct: I can treat every firearm as loaded, keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, keep my finger off the trigger until I am ready to shoot, and be certain of my target and what is beyond it, and I handle firearms only with a qualified instructor.

source.quote: Be certain of your target and what is beyond it.

changes.text: I can treat every firearm as loaded, keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, keep my finger off the trigger until I am ready to shoot, and be certain of my target and what is beyond it, and I handle firearms only with a qualified instructor.

findings.statement: I can check that a firearm is unloaded, load and unload it safely and hold it with a steady stance and grip.
findings.why: Handling, loading and owning a firearm needs a licence or certificate in many countries, with age limits, and the ladder never says so, though the skill is offered as something to practise in real life. CLAUDE.md asks the project to say plainly when a law limits something. Great Britain is one example; Canada (a possession licence) and Australia (a firearms licence) are others.
findings.correct: Where the law lets me and under a qualified instructor, I can check that a firearm is unloaded, load and unload it safely, and hold it with a steady stance and grip.

source.date: Firearms Act 1968 s.1, revised text up to date to 2026-11-15
source.quote: to have in his possession, or to purchase or acquire, a firearm to which this section applies without holding a firearm certificate in force at the time

changes.text: I can check that a firearm is unloaded, load and unload it safely, and hold it with a steady stance and grip, under a qualified instructor and where the law allows.

source.date: Firearms Act 1968 s.1, revised text up to date to 2026-11-15

findings.note: Same content, reordered so the statement starts "I can"; "where the law allows" is the general legal wording the review brief asks for.

findings.statement: I can safely deal with a simple stoppage the way I was taught, clean and store the firearm, and follow range commands without the guide.
findings.why: "Store the firearm" says nothing about how. Storage that keeps children and other unauthorised people away from guns prevents deaths and is a legal condition in many places; in Great Britain it is a condition of every firearm certificate. Idaho Fish and Game (https://idfg.idaho.gov/press/field-hunting-safety-reminders, 2013-11-05): "Store firearms and ammunition separately."
findings.correct: I can safely deal with a simple stoppage the way I was taught, keeping the muzzle pointed safely, clean the firearm, and store it unloaded and locked away from anyone not allowed to use it, with the ammunition stored separately as the law where I live requires, and I follow range commands without the guide.

source.date: Home Office Firearms security handbook 2020, updated 2021-01-20
source.quote: It is a condition of the issue of a firearm certificate that the firearms and shotguns to which the certificate relates must be stored securely at all times so as to prevent, so far as is reasonably practicable, access to the guns by unauthorised persons.

changes.text: I can safely deal with a simple stoppage the way I was taught, keeping the muzzle pointed safely, clean the firearm, and store it unloaded and locked away from anyone not allowed to use it, with the ammunition stored separately as the law where I live requires, and I follow range commands without the guide.

source.date: Home Office Firearms security handbook 2020, updated 2021-01-20

findings.statement: I can follow the safety steps for a mounted weapon: check it is safe, clear the firing zone and call out before firing.
findings.why: Written as a skill to learn in real life, but in real life mounted and automatic weapons belong to armed forces and specially authorised users: private ownership is banned or tightly restricted in most countries. In the US it is unlawful except under narrow exceptions (government use, and machine guns lawfully held before the 1986 cut-off). The game statements can stay, but the real-life twin needs to say so, or the skill should be marked game-only.
findings.correct: Keep the game statement, and add for real life: In real life, gunnery is learned only in the armed forces or in a simulator; owning or firing mounted or automatic weapons is banned or tightly restricted for private people in most countries.

findings.statement: I can make beer or wine safely with sanitised equipment and know why the sealed vessel matters.

"Know why the sealed vessel matters" teaches the opposite of the airlock's job, and someone who screws a lid onto a glass jug of fermenting wine can be cut by flying glass.

source.quote: Keep the refrigerator temperature at or below 40° F (4° C).

changes.text: I can keep raw meat at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder and apart from other food, and clean up properly afterwards.

findings.statement: I can grow a wide range of crops well and judge soil by touch, smell and sight.
findings.why: Touch, smell and sight judge texture and organic matter, but cannot detect contamination such as lead, common near old buildings and roads. An Expert grower should know when only a lab test answers the question, before growing food on unknown ground.
findings.correct: I can grow a wide range of crops well, judge soil by touch, smell and sight, and know when to send a sample for a lab test, since contamination such as lead cannot be seen.

source.quote: Knowing how much lead is in your soil is a good place to start

changes.text: I can grow a wide range of crops well, judge soil by touch, smell and sight, and know when to send a sample for a lab test, since contamination such as lead cannot be seen.

findings.statement: I can bake in a wood or camp oven and manage its heat.
findings.why: A camp oven heated by charcoal or a gas stove makes carbon monoxide; used in a tent, a garage or indoors it can kill. The statement gives no place rule.
findings.correct: I can bake in a wood oven or a camp oven (a camp oven only outdoors, never in a tent or indoors) and manage its heat.

source.quote: Never burn charcoal indoors.

changes.text: I can bake in a wood oven or a camp oven (a camp oven only outdoors, never in a tent or indoors) and manage its heat.

findings.statement: I can run a full bake for forty people to a standard
findings.why: "To a standard" names no standard that the learner or an assessor can check, unlike the other Expert statements in this group (cooking s5_a names food kept safe throughout). For forty people the standard should include even baking and allergen labelling. (The text is also the design doc's own example, so the doc would change with it; the baking statements also lack the full stop the others have.)
findings.correct: I can run a full bake for forty people, on time, with every loaf evenly baked through and every allergen labelled.

source.quote: Fast, excellent work with no prompts

changes.text: I can run a full bake for forty people, on time, with every loaf evenly baked through and every allergen labelled.

findings.statement: I can put on helmet, eye and ear protection and chaps, and keep clear while someone experienced fells a tree.
findings.why: "Keep clear" gives a novice no distance. The felling danger zone is set by distance, and a falling tree, or one that kicks back off its stump, reaches people who think they are clear.
findings.correct: I can put on a helmet, eye and ear protection and chaps, and stay at least two tree lengths away while someone experienced fells a tree.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 302); read 2026-11-14
source.quote: A safe working distance of two tree lengths must be maintained, unless exceptional conditions and a comprehensive risk assessment dictate otherwise.

changes.text: I can put on a helmet, eye and ear protection and chaps, and stay at least two tree lengths away while someone experienced fells a tree.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 302); read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can trim and cut up a small fallen tree into lengths with a hand saw, standing safely.
findings.why: A Beginner does starter procedures alone (skills.md). A fallen tree is often under tension or compression, or can roll, and "standing safely" does not say how: which side to stand, which side to cut first, and which trees to leave alone. Releasing tension is only taught at Proficient (s4_a).
findings.correct: I can trim and cut up a small fallen tree that lies flat and is not bent or caught, using a hand saw, standing on the uphill side, cutting the compressed side first, and leaving any springy or trapped trunk to someone trained.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 304); read 2026-11-14
source.quote: When cross-cutting on slopes, work on the uphill side of logs if there is a risk of the timber rolling. Reduce excessive tension by first making a cut on the compression side of the log

changes.text: I can trim and cut up a small fallen tree that lies flat and is not bent or caught, using a hand saw, standing on the uphill side, cutting the compressed side first, and leaving any springy or trapped trunk to someone trained.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 304); read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can spot and release tension in a tree that is under strain, and deal with one that is caught or leaning wrongly.
findings.why: "Deal with one that is caught" invites improvising with a hung-up tree, one of the commonest ways tree workers die. The usual improvisations (felling another tree onto it, cutting the tree holding it, climbing it, working under it) are exactly what safety guides forbid.
findings.correct: I can spot and release tension safely in a tree that is under strain, and bring down a hung-up tree with a felling lever, turning tool or winch, never by felling another tree onto it, cutting the tree that holds it, climbing it or working under it.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 302); read 2026-11-14
source.quote: Do not: fell the supporting tree in an attempt to free the hung-up tree; climb a hung-up tree; fell another tree across the hung-up tree in an attempt to dislodge it; walk or work under a hung-up tree

changes.text: I can spot and release tension safely in a tree that is under strain, and bring down a hung-up tree with a felling lever, turning tool or winch, never by felling another tree onto it, cutting the tree that holds it, climbing it or working under it.

source.date: October 2018 (Health and Safety Authority, Ireland, IFSG 302); read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can wear a helmet, eye and ear protection and a dust mask, and keep clear of loose rock while following the guide.
findings.why: Rock and quarry dust carries respirable crystalline silica. A "dust mask" in everyday speech is often a nuisance or comfort mask, which gives no real protection. The statement needs a rated, fitted respirator.
findings.correct: I can wear a helmet, eye and ear protection and a fitted respirator rated for fine dust (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask), and keep clear of loose rock while following the guide.

source.quote: Some retailers also sell products known as nuisance dust masks or comfort masks that look like dust respirators but are not marked with CE or with any standard.

changes.text: I can wear a helmet, eye and ear protection and a fitted respirator rated for fine dust (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask), and keep clear of loose rock while following the guide.

findings.statement: I can plan a dig or quarry face so that it is stable, drains water, and has a clear way out.
findings.why: Planning a stable dig is presented as a solo Competent skill with no supports, no safe batter angle and no inspection. Trench and face collapses kill. Where the law applies to the work, a competent person must inspect the supports.
findings.correct: I can plan a dig or quarry face so that its sides are supported or cut back to a safe angle, it drains water and has a clear way out, and I have a competent person inspect it before anyone works in it.

source.quote: No ground can be relied upon to stand unsupported in all circumstances.

changes.text: I can plan a dig or quarry face so that its sides are supported or cut back to a safe angle, it drains water and has a clear way out, and I have a competent person inspect it before anyone works in it.

findings.statement: I can sort metals by sight and by simple tests and skim slag off a melt.
findings.why: Sorting scrap is the point to reject coated metal. Melting galvanised or painted scrap gives off fumes that cause metal fume fever (and lead or cadmium coatings are worse). The statement teaches sorting with no word on fumes.
findings.correct: I can sort metals by sight and by simple tests, set aside galvanised, painted or coated scrap and unknown alloys whose fumes can make me ill, and skim slag off a melt.

source.quote: Metal fume fever is usually linked to welding or hot work on galvanised metals.

changes.text: I can sort metals by sight and by simple tests, set aside galvanised, painted or coated scrap and unknown alloys whose fumes can make me ill, and skim slag off a melt.

findings.statement: I can clean and clamp joints properly and avoid welding near anything that can burn.
findings.why: "Avoid welding near anything that can burn" is vague, and it misses the fatal case: welding or cutting a drum, tank or container that once held fuel. Residue in an "empty" drum explodes.
findings.correct: I can clean and clamp joints properly, move or cover anything that can burn well clear of the sparks, keep an extinguisher and someone watching for fire, and never weld or cut a drum, tank or container that has held fuel or chemicals unless someone trained has made it safe.

source.quote: Tanks and drums that seem to be ‘empty’ usually still have residues in the bottom, in seams and other crevices. Just a teaspoon of petrol in a drum can be enough to cause an explosion

changes.text: I can clean and clamp joints properly, move or cover anything that can burn well clear of the sparks, keep an extinguisher and someone watching for fire, and never weld or cut a drum, tank or container that has held fuel or chemicals unless someone trained has made it safe.

findings.statement: I can wear eye protection, tie back hair and loose clothing, and follow the steps to make one simple cut on a lathe or mill.
findings.why: The novice lathe and mill statement covers hair and loose clothing but not gloves, rings or watches. A glove caught by a rotating chuck or drill pulls the hand in, a leading cause of serious workshop injuries.
findings.correct: I can wear eye protection, tie back hair, take off gloves, rings and watches, keep loose clothing clear, and follow the steps to make one simple cut on a lathe or mill.

source.quote: Many serious accidents that occur in engineering workshops could be avoided if the wearing of gloves was prevented whilst working in close proximity to rotating machinery such as drills and lathes.

changes.text: I can wear eye protection, tie back hair, take off gloves, rings and watches, keep loose clothing clear, and follow the steps to make one simple cut on a lathe or mill.

findings.statement: I can wedge clay and make a simple pinch pot, wearing a dust mask while handling dry clay.
findings.why: Dry clay and glaze dust contain crystalline silica. The real control is keeping dust down (wet cleaning, never dry sweeping), and when dust cannot be avoided a rated respirator; a generic "dust mask" may be a nuisance mask that does nothing.
findings.correct: I can wedge clay and make a simple pinch pot, clean dry clay dust with water or a filtered vacuum instead of sweeping, and wear a rated respirator (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask) when dust cannot be avoided.

source.quote: These are not intended for use when a respirator should be worn. You should never use a nuisance dust mask instead

changes.text: I can wedge clay and make a simple pinch pot, clean dry clay dust with water or a filtered vacuum instead of sweeping, and wear a rated respirator (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask) when dust cannot be avoided.

findings.statement: I can make bricks, tiles or a ceramic water filter that works.
findings.why: "A ceramic water filter that works" invites people to drink filtered water as safe. A clay filter can remove bacteria and protozoa, but filters of this kind do not reliably remove viruses, and a home-made one has not been tested. Drinking water must still be disinfected.
findings.correct: I can make bricks or tiles that hold up, and a ceramic water filter whose flow I test, and I still disinfect the water it makes (for example with chlorine), because a filter does not reliably remove viruses.

source.date: last updated April 23, 2025 (CDC Yellow Book); read 2026-11-14
source.quote: Many filters do not reliably remove viruses

changes.text: I can make bricks or tiles that hold up, and a ceramic water filter whose flow I test, and I still disinfect the water it makes (for example with chlorine), because a filter does not reliably remove viruses.

source.date: last updated April 23, 2025 (CDC Yellow Book); read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can repair a damaged board by replacing parts and fixing broken tracks.
findings.why: Repairing a board says nothing about power or stored energy. Boards from mains equipment (power supplies, microwave ovens, TVs) hold a dangerous charge in capacitors after unplugging.
findings.correct: I can repair a damaged board by replacing parts and fixing broken tracks, with the power off and stored energy in capacitors and batteries released first; mains power supplies and microwave ovens I leave to someone trained.

source.quote: You can be reasonably sure that your electrical equipment is safe to work on if all sources of energy ... have been securely isolated and any stored energy has been released from the equipment.

changes.text: I can repair a damaged board by replacing parts and fixing broken tracks, with the power off and stored energy in capacitors and batteries released first; mains power supplies and microwave ovens I leave to someone trained.

findings.statement: I can work safely at height with ladders and scaffold and brace a wall while it is built.
findings.why: Working safely at height on ladders and scaffold is placed at Proficient, but the Competent stage (s3_a) already builds a shed roof, which is work at height. Roof work is among the deadliest construction tasks, so height safety must come before the roof.
findings.correct: Move to Beginner (before the Competent shed roof): I can set up and climb a ladder safely and tell when scaffold or edge protection is needed. Keep "brace a wall while it is built" at Proficient.

source.quote: High risk: almost one in five deaths in construction work involve roof work.

changes.text: I can set up and climb a ladder safely and tell when scaffold or edge protection is needed.
I can work safely at height from scaffold and brace a wall while it is built.

findings.note: The ladder half moves to Beginner as a new statement; Proficient keeps the scaffold and the bracing.

findings.statement: I can lead the building of a sound house or ship section to a standard, with no prompts.
findings.why: Leading the building of a house is presented with no mention of building approval, permits or inspections, which most places require for a new dwelling.
findings.correct: I can lead the building of a sound house or ship section to a standard, with no prompts, getting the building approval or permits it needs and passing its inspections.

source.quote: You must check if you need approval before you construct or change buildings in certain ways.

changes.text: I can lead the building of a sound house or ship section to a standard, with no prompts, getting the building approval or permits it needs and passing its inspections.

findings.statement: I can wear eye protection, gloves and a dust mask, and mix mortar following the steps.
findings.why: Mixing dry mortar and cement raises fine dust (cement and sand). "A dust mask" may be read as a nuisance mask that does not protect; name a rated respirator.
findings.correct: I can wear eye protection, gloves and a rated respirator (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask), and mix mortar following the steps.

source.quote: Some retailers also sell products known as nuisance dust masks or comfort masks that look like dust respirators but are not marked with CE or with any standard.

changes.text: I can wear eye protection, gloves and a rated respirator (FFP3 or equivalent, not a nuisance dust mask), and mix mortar following the steps.

findings.statement: I can use a tester to prove a circuit dead, and never work on a live one.
findings.why: A Beginner works alone (skills.md). Proving dead without proving the tester works, before and after, is the classic fatal mistake: a failed tester reads "dead" on a live circuit. The guidance also says which testers to use (two-pole testers, not multimeters or volt sticks) and that training is essential.
findings.correct: I can prove a circuit dead with a proper two-pole voltage tester, checking the tester on a proving unit before and after the test, testing every conductor, and I never work on a live circuit.

source.quote: It will be necessary to test the instrument before and after use. This may be done by means of a proving unit with a low power output.

changes.text: I can prove a circuit dead with a proper two-pole voltage tester, checking the tester on a proving unit before and after the test, testing every conductor, and I never work on a live circuit.

findings.statement: I can wire a simple circuit with a switch, a light and a fuse or breaker without the guide.
findings.why: Wiring a circuit with a breaker "without the guide" is presented with no word on the law. In England a new circuit is notifiable building work (a building notice before work, or a registered electrician); other countries require a permit and inspection, and some allow only licensed electricians to do mains work.
findings.correct: I can wire a simple circuit with a switch, a light and a fuse or breaker on a training board without the guide, and before touching a real installation I follow the local rules (a permit, notifying building control, or a licensed electrician).

source.quote: A person intending to carry out building work ... is required to give a building notice or deposit full plans where the work consists of-- (a) the installation of a new circuit

changes.text: I can wire a simple circuit with a switch, a light and a fuse or breaker on a training board without the guide, and before touching a real installation I follow the local rules (a permit, notifying building control, or a licensed electrician).

findings.statement: I can connect a solar panel and battery system so that it is protected.
findings.why: Solar panels produce voltage whenever light falls on them and cannot be switched off at the panel, and batteries can deliver very high fault currents. The statement treats a home solar and battery system as a solo Proficient job with no word on either hazard or on licensed installers.
findings.correct: I can connect a small solar panel and battery system so that it is protected, covering the panels while I work because they are live in daylight; a system wired into a home I install under a licensed installer, as local rules require.

source.date: last updated February 21, 2025 (US Department of Energy); read 2026-11-14
source.quote: utilize properly licensed installers to ensure the safety of these systems

changes.text: I can connect a small solar panel and battery system so that it is protected, covering the panels while I work because they are live in daylight; a system wired into a home I leave to a licensed installer, or work under one, where local rules require it.

source.date: last updated February 21, 2025 (US Department of Energy); read 2026-11-14

findings.note: The last clause is reworded to read plainly; the review's summary says the "live in daylight" wording is common practice with no quoted source, kept because it is plain physics (a lit panel makes voltage).

findings.statement: I can plan, install and test a whole system to a standard, safely and with no prompts.
findings.why: Planning and installing a whole electrical system is presented as a matter of skill alone. Whole-installation work is notifiable or licensed work almost everywhere.
findings.correct: I can plan, install and test a whole system to the local wiring rules, with the permit, notification or licence they require, safely and with no prompts.

source.quote: is required to give a building notice or deposit full plans where the work consists of-- (a) the installation of a new circuit; (b) the replacement of a consumer unit

changes.text: I can plan, install and test a whole system to the local wiring rules, with the permit, notification or licence they require, safely and with no prompts.

findings.statement: I can size a heater or cooler for a room and set it up without the guide.
findings.why: Setting up a heater "without the guide" covers fuel-burning heaters, whose wrong installation or venting causes carbon monoxide poisoning. The statement needs venting, a CO alarm and professional installation for fuel appliances.
findings.correct: I can size a heater or cooler for a room and set it up without the guide; a fuel-burning heater I have installed by a qualified person, vented as its maker says, with a carbon monoxide alarm fitted.

source.date: no date shown on page; read 2026-11-14
source.quote: Make sure appliances are installed and operated according to the manufacturer's instructions and local building codes. Most appliances should be installed by qualified professionals.

changes.text: I can size a heater or cooler for a room and set it up without the guide; a fuel-burning heater I have installed by a qualified person, vented as its maker says, with a carbon monoxide alarm fitted.

source.date: no date shown on page; read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can set up a heat pump or a heat recovery fan and check that it works.
findings.why: Setting up a heat pump usually means connecting and charging a refrigerant circuit, which legally needs a qualified technician (F-gas qualifications in the UK; similar refrigerant certification elsewhere).
findings.correct: I can choose and place a heat pump or a heat recovery fan and check that it works; connecting or charging the heat pump's refrigerant circuit I leave to a certified refrigerant technician.

source.quote: For RACHP systems you must have qualifications to: install new systems; service and maintain systems; check for leaks

changes.text: I can choose and place a heat pump or a heat recovery fan and check that it works; connecting or charging the heat pump's refrigerant circuit I leave to a certified refrigerant technician.

findings.statement: I can tell the signs of too little oxygen or too much carbon dioxide and call for help quickly.
findings.why: The statement teaches people to rely on noticing the signs of low oxygen. Low oxygen usually gives no warning a person can sense before they collapse; only a meter or alarm warns in time. The same is true in real confined spaces.
findings.correct: I can read the oxygen and carbon dioxide meters and alarms, know that too little oxygen can knock me out with no warning I would notice, and leave and call for help as soon as a reading or alarm says so.

source.date: CSB Safety Bulletin No. 2003-10-B, June 2003; read 2026-11-14
source.quote: The exposed person has no warning and cannot sense that the oxygen level is too low.

changes.text: I can read the oxygen and carbon dioxide meters and alarms, know that too little oxygen can knock me out with no warning I would notice, and leave and call for help as soon as a reading or alarm says so.

source.date: CSB Safety Bulletin No. 2003-10-B, June 2003; read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can pick the right knots, pulleys and rope for a load and rig a lift without the guide.
findings.why: Choosing rope, pulleys and slings for a lift (Competent) depends on knowing the load's weight and each item's marked safe working load, but that is placed later, at Proficient (s4_b). A rigger who cannot estimate the weight should not be rigging lifts alone.
findings.correct: I can work out a load's weight, pick knots, pulleys, slings and rope whose marked safe working load covers it, and rig a simple lift without the guide. (Move the weight estimate here from Proficient.)

source.quote: Don't... exceed the safe working load of machinery or accessories like chains, slings and grabs.

changes.text: I can work out a load's weight, pick knots, pulleys, slings and rope whose marked safe working load covers it, and rig a simple lift without the guide.

findings.note: The reviewer's bracketed pointer (the weight estimate moves here from Proficient) is a note, not words for the statement; Proficient's s4_b keeps the harder part (sling angles).

findings.statement: I can work out a load's weight and choose gear with a safe margin.
findings.why: "A safe margin" cannot be checked. The checkable rules are: never exceed the marked safe working load, and allow for the extra load sling angles put on each leg; do not lift if the weight is in doubt.
findings.correct: I can work out a load's weight, including the extra force that wide sling angles put on each leg, and never use gear beyond its marked safe working load; if I doubt the weight, I do not lift.

source.quote: Remember that the load in the legs of a sling increases as the angle between the legs increases

changes.text: I can work out a load's weight, including the extra force that wide sling angles put on each leg, and never use gear beyond its marked safe working load; if I doubt the weight, I do not lift.

findings.statement: I can change a tyre and a filter and check brakes and belts.
findings.why: A Beginner does this alone. Changing a tyre and checking brakes means a raised vehicle with a wheel off; vehicles falling off jacks are the main cause of deaths in vehicle repair. The statement does not say to use axle stands or never to rely on a jack.
findings.correct: I can change a tyre and a filter and check brakes and belts, putting the vehicle on axle stands on firm, level ground whenever a wheel is off or any part of me goes under it; I never rely on a jack alone.

source.quote: vehicles are always properly supported - do not rely on jacks alone

changes.text: I can change a tyre and a filter and check brakes and belts, putting the vehicle on axle stands on firm, level ground whenever a wheel is off or any part of me goes under it; I never rely on a jack alone.

findings.statement: I can unplug a broken item, look it over, and follow the steps to fix a simple fault.
findings.why: A novice told "unplug it and fix a simple fault" is not warned that some unplugged items keep a dangerous charge (microwave ovens, mains power supplies, TVs).
findings.correct: I can unplug a broken item, look it over, and follow the steps to fix a simple fault, and I know that some items, such as microwave ovens and power supplies, hold a dangerous charge after unplugging, so I leave those to someone trained.

source.quote: any stored energy has been released from the equipment

changes.text: I can unplug a broken item, look it over, and follow the steps to fix a simple fault, and I know that some items, such as microwave ovens and power supplies, hold a dangerous charge after unplugging, so I leave those to someone trained.

findings.statement: I can lift and carry goods with a straight back and label a box, following the steps.
findings.why: "With a straight back" is folk advice. Official guidance prefers a slight bend of back, hips and knees, the load close to the waist, no twisting, and help for heavy loads.
findings.correct: I can lift and carry goods with the load close to my waist, a slight bend in my back, hips and knees, no twisting, and ask for help with anything heavy, and label a box, following the steps.

source.quote: Slight bending of your back, hips and knees at the start of the lift is preferable to either fully flexing your back (stooping) or fully flexing your hips and knees (full/deep squatting).

changes.text: I can lift and carry goods with the load close to my waist, a slight bend in my back, hips and knees, no twisting, and ask for help with anything heavy, and label a box, following the steps.

findings.statement: I can drive on a quiet road, keep a safe distance and obey the signs.
findings.why: A Beginner works alone (skills.md), so this reads as driving on a public road alone. A learner needs a provisional licence or permit and a qualified supervising driver; driving alone without a licence is illegal almost everywhere.
findings.correct: I can drive on a quiet road with my learner's licence and a qualified driver supervising me, keep a safe distance and obey the signs.

source.quote: You must have a provisional driving licence for Great Britain or Northern Ireland when you’re learning to drive or ride. You must be supervised when you're learning to drive a car.

changes.text: I can drive on a quiet road with my learner's licence and a qualified driver supervising me, keep a safe distance and obey the signs.

findings.statement: I can drive in traffic and on rough tracks without the guide, keeping a safe speed for the conditions.
findings.why: Driving in traffic without a guide is presented with no mention of passing the test and holding a full licence for that kind of vehicle.
findings.correct: With a full licence for the vehicle, I can drive in traffic and on rough tracks without the guide, keeping a safe speed for the conditions.

source.quote: You must be supervised when you’re learning to drive a car.

changes.text: I can drive in traffic and on rough tracks without the guide, with a full licence for the vehicle, keeping a safe speed for the conditions.

findings.correct: Once my instructor has signed me off for solo, I can plan a short flight, check the weather, and fly it and land alone.

findings.correct: With a flight instructor certificate, I can write a flying lesson, train other pilots and assess them.

findings.statement: I can fly safely around people and obstacles and keep clear of other aircraft.
findings.why: "Fly safely around people" presents closeness to people as a matter of skill. Most rules set a minimum distance from uninvolved people and forbid flying over crowds, whatever the pilot's skill.
findings.correct: I can fly safely around obstacles, keep the distance from people the rules set where I fly (in the UK, 50 m from uninvolved people for most drones, and never over a crowd), and keep clear of other aircraft.

source.date: UK CAA Drone and Model Aircraft Code, page build 2026-08-20; read 2026-11-14
source.quote: You must keep a minimum horizontal distance of 50m between your drone or model aircraft and people.

changes.text: I can fly safely around obstacles, keep as far from people as the rules where I fly require, never fly over a crowd, and keep clear of other aircraft.

source.date: UK CAA Drone and Model Aircraft Code, page build 2026-08-20; read 2026-11-14

findings.note: Generalised: the UK distance (50 m from uninvolved people for most drones, from the UK CAA source) stays in the source quote rather than the statement, which holds in any country.

findings.statement: I can run my full routine with unlit props first, and only then a lit one, always with a trained spotter and a fire blanket present.
findings.why: This is the first lit spin, but no stage in the ladder teaches fuelling: dipping the wick, spinning off the excess fuel away from the area, keeping fuel capped and away from flame, and never using petrol. Unspun fuel flies off burning onto the performer and the audience. Fire codes require excess fuel removed before ignition.
findings.correct: Add before the first lit spin (Competent): I can fuel a prop safely, dipping the wick, spinning off the excess fuel into a spin-off bucket well away from the performance area, keeping the fuel capped and away from flame, and never using petrol. Then: I can run my full routine with unlit props first, and only then a lit one, always with a trained spotter, a fire blanket or wet towel and an extinguisher present.

source.date: Portland Fire & Rescue FMO Policy, Fire Performance Art, revision 8/18; read 2026-11-14
source.quote: Excess fuel shall be removed from devices in an approved manner before they are ignited or used in front of an audience. A "spin out bucket" shall be utilized to spin off any excess fuel

findings.statement: I can adjust the setup for different spaces, such as indoors or crowded venues, and decide when not to perform.
findings.why: Performing indoors or at crowded venues is treated as a setup decision. Many cities require a fire performance permit, approved distances, safety staff and an extinguisher, and indoor shows need the venue's and fire authority's approval.
findings.correct: I can adjust the setup for different spaces, such as indoors or crowded venues, get the venue's and fire authority's permission (a permit in many places), and decide when not to perform.

source.date: Portland Fire & Rescue FMO Policy, Fire Performance Art, revision 8/18; read 2026-11-14

findings.statement: I can spot when a disagreement is too serious or unsafe for me and ask for help.
findings.why: Recognising when a dispute is unsafe (threats, violence, abuse) comes at Competent, after the Beginner stage already questions both sides alone. Screening for danger comes before trying to settle anything; formal family mediation itself is waived where there has been domestic abuse.
findings.correct: Move to Beginner (before s2_b): I can spot when a disagreement involves threats, violence or abuse, or is too serious for me, and get help instead of trying to settle it myself.
